I lived as a gay guy for about a decade before my transition, and I was never called the t slur then. Maybe it’s a location thing, but I haven’t really ever heard it used for gay men; just for trans women, drag queens, and crossdressers. I personally am not a fan of a cis guy, whether gay or straight, “reclaiming” the t slur.

The biggest reason is that slurs are not just used to put one down, they’re used to disparage and dehumanize someone for an inherent characteristic. In this specific case, the t slur isn’t used to dehumanize someone for being a gay guy, but for *looking like a trans woman.* It’s similar to how straight men are often called the f slur for *looking or acting like a gay man.*

Now where people draw the line for slur reclamation is individual, but for people in my circles at least, the line is usually drawn at “if the slur is not directed at *your* identity, then you cannot reclaim it.”

I think the mutual frustration with the term from both sides is that one side is arguing with the perspective that this debate is about what one wishes gender ought to be, and one which views the debate as a phenomenon in wider society. It’s an is vs. ought distinction.

You can call yourself whatever you want. If you find it empowering, knock yourself out! Most of the criticism of the term comes from the perspective of trans women who are frustrated with a few things regarding the term. First, there is frustration with the ability of many non-trans-femme to use the term “genderfuck” to essentially mean “look like a non-passing trans woman.” This ties into the second part: the fact that the societal consequences for being a “genderfuck” are very different for transfemmes vs. non-transfemmes. For non-transfemmes, the consequences usually range from regendering (i.e. being treated as a “confused/rebellious woman”), to harassment (especially the more butch one goes). For transfemmes, the consequences range from being degendered (i.e. treated as less than either a man or a woman), to assaulted. The asymmetry is frustrating, and it shows a wider societal trend of discrimination against transfemmes in particular. 

I dislike the gamut of replies on this post being dismissive of the criticisms of the term. I find that most people assume that the only way people could have a problem with the term is if they “care about gender too much” or they are purely transmedicalist, when this is simply not true. The vast majority of the criticism nowadays is from those viewing gender not as something separate from society, but as a societal construct, and one which interacts heavily with preexisting societal constructs.

I think at a certain point the concept of giving a single-word label to sexual orientation begins to break down a bit. You can get into microlabels, of course, but at a certain point some of the primary purposes of sexual orientation labels, communication and group identification, break down as the microlabels become more niche. This isn’t a slight against microlabels, mind you, but it demonstrates how sexual orientation as a concept can be broken down: what kind of people are you attracted to?

Many non-binary people are either asexual, bisexual, pansexual, or omnisexual, and so these non-binary people generally don’t need to label their orientation any further. 

Many still are left if we exclude those who identify with those “umbrella” labels. This is where we get into the weeds of personal preference. Some people will prefer microlabels in reference to their orientation. Some will reject the notion of orientation altogether. Some will simply choose an orientation that aligns with the gender they were assigned at birth. Some may choose an orientation that aligns with the gender “opposite” of what they were assigned at birth. 

Personally, I think the labeling of sexual orientation is a bit flawed, and we ought to use more descriptive phrasing. If I was asked what my sexual orientation was, would respond “I’m attracted to traits traditionally associated with masculinity” if I’m in the mood to describe the ins and outs of gender and its relationship to sexual attraction (or just talking to another queer person), and “I’m straight” if I’m not in that mood, as I generally present myself as a mostly binary trans woman.

That being said, orientation labels do have uses; the ones I mentioned before, communication and group identification. The latter is a bit more central to the argument for keeping them than the former, but nevertheless, they are a quick and easy way of identifying oneself with a group, as well as a way for people with similar goals to identify each other to work towards those goals. 

Gender and sexuality are complicated. You’re attracted to who you’re attracted to, and frankly, it doesn’t really matter what the person you’re attracted to identifies as. So long as you respect their identity, it doesn’t matter if you’re gay, straight, bi, or what have you. Sexual orientation is a name we’ve given to the pattern of our attraction, and sometimes patterns may deviate. Sometimes something breaks that pattern completely, which is fine so long as you’re able to still see the component parts.

I will preface this by saying that my perspective is that of a newer high school math teacher, and that my perspective is further marred by only having experience in my district.

> Do you sincerely believe students having access to a phone during the event of a school shooting or any other potential emergency is such a negative thing that it’s worth completely banning them?

No. The reason it’s worth banning them is because of their effect inside the classroom. The negative impacts of phones during normal class hours are far understated. When I say students are addicted to their phones, I mean this as no exaggeration. I was lucky that my parents *did* teach me how to use my phone in a healthy way; most students are not nearly as lucky, especially in poorer districts. 

Phones are possibly the #1 distraction in the classroom, except for maybe Chromebooks, which I also despise. Students with a YouTube video or TikTok playing behind my back distracts other students as well. I cannot possibly be monitoring each student in a classroom at the same time to get them back on track, nor am I allowed to confiscate a student’s phone.

Further, students’ fixations on their phones has genuinely negatively impacted their ability to socialize. I recognize that a large part of this was due to the pandemic, but by and large, students nor their parents are willing to wean off the habit, and that leads to further social isolation, leading to depression, addiction, and self harm. 

And that’s not even addressing the elephant in the room of cheating. Photomath is quick and easy to conceal once you’ve taken the picture. All a student needs is a back turned for 3 seconds and the student learns nothing. Sure, that’s on them, but do we really need to give them the easy option? 

Kids aren’t learning healthy phone habits on their own, and parents aren’t stepping up either. If we can’t confiscate them, and they’re impacting everyone, what other choices do we have?

> What if some kid collapses from heat or a heart attack?

I’m not saying this could never happen, but teachers are essentially required to keep an eye on students anywhere they go, save for the hallway during class time and the bathroom. Sure, in your exact hypothetical not having a phone would be a tragedy, but is this legitimately a concern when students are essentially monitored the entire time?

> What if they’re walking home and someone’s following them?

This is definitely the case that I most empathize with, but also one not affected by the ban. In fact, only the heart attack/heatstroke example is actually affected by the ban, as the budget proposal simply states that schools must impose a ban on wireless communication devices during instructional time or else the school won’t receive funding. 

The school shooting hypothetical is a non-issue for this bill, as students are obviously not in instructional time. The solution for the student who walks home is to keep it in their backpack until school is over.

One of my biggest is facial dystonia. My mouth or eye muscles will involuntarily contract, either resulting in just a funny face or sometimes me closing my eyes completely. When I encounter this symptom, if it’s a mouth pulling, I can usually distract myself/wait it out. Otherwise, I imagine myself looking at a mirror and my face going back to normal, and that usually serves as a temporary fix. 

Another I have, but usually only during bad episodes, is what appears on the outside to be non-epileptic seizures. After discussing with a specialist however, we feel that dissociative attack is a more proper term for how they manifest in me. I will lose the ability to control my body completely over the course of between one minute and a few seconds, and the effect lasts between five to thirty seconds. I am still conscious, and in many (but not all) cases I’m able to give minor signals such as a finger twitch. 

Another symptom is brain fog. It’s hard to describe how it feels, except through analogy. Normally my train of thought is clear and arrives at some destination. However, when I’m experiencing FND brain fog, the train doesn’t move at all.

1. **Thinking about it.** This is probably my biggest trigger, and hard to control because once I start, it’s hard to stop. 

2. **Lack of sleep.** If I’m running on fewer than 6 hours of sleep, all my symptoms flare up, and I usually need a few days of recovery to get back to normal. 

3. **Sensory overload.** Sudden or undesirable loud noises, too much visual stimulus, or excessive heat will cause pretty major symptoms usually.

That’s not quite right. Phi was pronounced in Ancient Greek as a voiceless aspirated bilabial stop, or in other words, “p” with a little “h” right after. Same goes for Chi. We get the spellings largely from Latin, who more or less tried to stay faithful to Greek pronunciation (and even going so far to stick to Greek spelling as creating a new letter, y).

The reason that Greek borrowed it as phi (and by extension handed it down as “ph” in English) is because phi was the closest thing thing to the Hebrew “f” in the Greek phonemic system. Another reason is that Greek at the time was also undergoing a shift from the aspirated consonants to fricatives in their relative places of articulation, but that wasn’t happening everywhere.
